recoveryDashboard.biteFact1: Pausing for 10 seconds before acting can weaken an impulsive urge.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact2: Urges work like waves: they rise, peak, then fade on their own within minutes.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact3: Naming a feeling ("I feel restless") helps your brain lower its intensity.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact4: Slow, deep breaths signal safety to your body and lower tension.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact5: Your environment shapes habits: keeping triggers out of reach makes healthy choices feel easier.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact6: Getting enough sleep strengthens your ability to manage urges the next day.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact7: Writing down what you feel helps your mind feel more organized.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact8: Progress is rarely a straight line. A hard day does not mean going backward.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact9: Switching activities for a few minutes is often enough to ride out a short urge.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact10: Talking to someone you trust can ease the weight of an urge almost immediately.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact11: Light movement like a short walk safely releases restless energy.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact12: A small, specific intention ("I close my laptop at 9") is easier to keep than a big resolution.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact13: The 'near-miss' feeling is designed to make your brain want another try, even though the odds never changed.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact14: Every gambling game carries a mathematical edge for the house; the longer you play, the more certain the loss.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact15: Terms like a site 'running hot' are marketing stories, not real patterns — every round stands alone.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact16: Chasing losses is the pattern that most reliably deepens them. Stopping is the only real exit from the minus.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact17: Games deliberately remove time cues; an outside alarm keeps you aware of how long you've been in.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact18: The strongest urges usually last only 3-5 minutes. Riding one out makes the next one easier.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact19: Your brain builds habits through repetition — every time you choose to pause, that new path gets stronger.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact20: Boredom is an underrated trigger. Keeping a ready list of alternatives takes its power away.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact21: Early 'winnings' are part of the design: they teach your brain to tag gambling as rewarding.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact22: Avoiding temptation isn't weakness — shaping your environment is the most effective self-control strategy.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact23: Stress narrows your view. When pressured, delay important decisions a few minutes until your breathing settles.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact24: Celebrating small wins (finishing one mission) sustains motivation better than one distant big target.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact25: A phone out of reach while studying lowers temptation more effectively than willpower alone.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact26: Guilt after a slip can itself trigger a repeat. Self-compassion works better than self-punishment.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact27: Body and mind shape each other: eating regularly keeps your emotions steadier through the day.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact28: Delaying 10 minutes is a secret weapon: most urges don't survive that long.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact29: Social media is full of winning stories that don't represent reality — losses rarely get posted.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact30: Borrowing money to play is the most serious signal. When that thought appears, it is time to reach for support.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact31: Tidying one small corner of your room gives a real, fast sense of control.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact32: Self-talk matters: 'I am learning to stop' feels different from 'I failed again'.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact33: Calm music lowers your heart rate and helps your body leave alert mode.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact34: Every day without gambling is real data that you can do this — your brain is writing that proof.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact35: Morning sunlight helps regulate your sleep rhythm, and good sleep strengthens self-control.
recoveryDashboard.biteFact36: Asking for help early is not defeat; it is the strategic move made by people who recover.
